newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST - Australian Business News - April 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Australian Business News - April 22.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

A sale to be announced today by the Victorian Government will be Australia's biggest privatisation so far - surpassing last year's A$4 billion sale of Commonwealth Bank shares. A consortium led by the United States-based CMS Energy Corp made a successful bid of more than A$4.7 billion for the 2,000 megawatt Loy Yang A power station and brown coal mine. Page 1.

In a move reflecting powerful fund managers' increasing dissatisfaction at several Australian Stock Exchange decisions, institutional investors are asking the Federal Government to establish an appeal of review body to oversee the ASX's regulation of listd companies. Page 1.

New South Wales Fair Trading Minister Faye Lo Po has called on the Federal Government to sign the ILO's convention on Home-Based Work in a bid to increase pressure on retailers and manufacturers to discontinue the exploitation of outworkers. Textile, Cloting and Footwear Union national secretary Tony Woolgar added to the call yesterday, saying the Union would prefer the death of industry in this country to the continued exploitation of such workers. Page 3.

In a long-awaited decision following a New South Wales Cabinet meeting yesterday which considered the privatisation of the State Totalisator Agency Board (TAB), the State Government will today announce the privatisation will go ahead, probably through a public float expected to raise up to A$1 billion. Page 21.

Mobil Oil Australia chairman and managing director PC Tan said yesterday the company's disappointing result for 1996 came after Mobil suspended all new capital investments in its fuel business amid uncertainty and confusion in the debate leading up to dergulation of the industry. Mobil posted a net profit of just A$75.4 million in the 12 months. Page 21.

Under a deal which would bring together Australia's two largest contract wine processors and deliver about 15 per cent of national wine production to the merged group, Orlando-Wyndham offshoot Simeon Wines Ltd is considering a A$200 million merger with wine processor Australian Vintage Ltd. Page 21.
THE AUSTRALIAN

In a surprise announcement from a company which less than 12 months ago announced it was moving into a consolidation phase, paper and packaging group Amcor Ltd is back on the expansion trail, with plans to spend A$200 million-plus in the next 12 to 18 monhs on acquisitions of significant size in Europe and the United States. Page 21.

The Australian Federation of Travel Agents warned Ansett yesterday that more than 90 per cent of its members would choose to sell Qantas air travel if Ansett goes ahead with plans to slash travel agent commission rates from 10 per cent to eight per cent for overseas travel and from five per cent to four per cent for domestic travel from May 1. Page 21.

According to a new report by the Federal Government's East Asia Analytical Unit, released yesterday by Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer, China's agricultural policy is at a stage where the Government can either pursue self-sufficiency in grain fo food security reasons, or opt for global competitive agriculture from super-efficient broadacre producers such as Australia. Page 21.

Production on the A$1 billion Laminaria-Corallina oil project in the Timor Sea is expected to commence in 1999 after the three partners in the project - Woodside Petroleum Ltd, BHP and Shell Australia - approved funds yesterday to build the world's largest floating production facility. Page 23.

Despite the recent political tension in Papua New Guinea and fallout from the Busang gold mine scandal in Indonesia, Highlands Pacific - a spin-off from Highlands Gold Ltd - launched the prospectus for a A$190 to A$210 million float, with underwriters to the float saying they expect the issue to close oversubscribed. Page 23.

Speaking after addressing a Securities Institute lunch in Sydney yesterday, Westpac chief executive Bob Joss said he was hopeful the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission would approve the bank's A$1.44 billion merger with the Bank of Melbourne, which he said would benefit Australia by helping lower business costs. Page 23.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

In one of this country's largest privatisation deals, the Loy Yang A power station, one of Victoria's four brown coal power stations, has been sold to a group headed by United States-based CMS Energy for a price believed to be about A$4.75 billion. Under the deal, the station will be half owned by CMS, with another 25 per cent owned by fellow American NRG Energy. Page 27.

Former electronics and telecommunications group AWA appears to have been dealt a devastating blow, with the New South Wales Government expected to announce today its plan to sell the State TAB through a A$1 billion public float, rather than through a trade sale, under which AWA was planning on buying the TAB. Page 27.

Speaking at a Securities Institute of Australia lunch yesterday, Westpac managing director Bob Joss said the bank saved A$38 million from the "synergies" involved in its takeover of West Australia's Challenge Bank, a deal he described as a "model" for bank mergers. The savings represented 45 per cent of Challenge's operating cost. Page 29.

The A$100 million wine producer Australian Vintage yesterday requested its shares be suspended on the Australian Stock Exchange pending confirmation of a possible takeover offer from Simeon Wines, which is 42 per cent-owned by French-controlled Orlando Wydham. Page 29.

According to a study by Michael Heffernan, a stockbroking analyst with FW Holst, private share ownership in Australia regained some lost ground in the last half of 1996 thanks to big floats such as that of National Mutual and the Commonwealth Bank, but reained well short of its record high of three-and-a-half years ago. Page 29.

American Express announced yesterday plans to offer a new low-interest credit card aimed at attracting the banks' Mastercard and Visa card bases. The new card will operate as a credit card, however it will offer a 13.85 per cent interest rate, about two prcentage points lower than all comparable products - if customers make their payments on time. Page 29.
THE AGE

Prime Minister John Howard yesterday asked the car industry to forward plans to amend its export facilitation scheme to make it comply with world trading rules. Howard has asked industry leaders to propose options to alter the scheme to meet the Uruguay Round's stricter rules on industry subsidies, or replace it with other assistance. Page B1.

Westpac Banking Corp managing director Bob Joss said yesterday that small business borrowers get one of the world's best deals from Australian banks and do not have restricted access to finance or punitively high interest rates. Joss's comments contradict the views of the Federal Government and small-business organisations. Page B1.

After several false starts, Highlands Pacific yesterday issued its prospectus for a $A190 million raising of the initial capital to boost the beginnings of the development of two world-class mining projects in Papua New Guinea. The company float has been created to acquire the non-gold assets of its predecessor Highlands Gold, and features an entitlements offer of 113.5 million shares plus a public offer of 76.5 million new shares at $A1 each. Page B1.

Telecommunications company Telstra's Aa2 long-term and Prime-1 short-term credit ratings were yesterday reaffirmed by ratings agency Moody's Investors Service after Friday's downgrading by the rival agency Standard & Poor. An S&P downgrade from AAA on Teltra's Australian dollar long-term debt to AA+ was triggered by Friday's Federal Government decision to take $3 billion as a special dividend before Telstra's partial privatisation. Page B3.

Talks with Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto later this month are expected to see Prime Minister John Howard reject Japan's decision to dump imports of Australian rice in third countries. Attempts by Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fisher to overturn the dumping policy on the grounds that it violates the spirit of GATT have been rebuffed by Japan. Page B3.

A low-interest card aimed at attracting the banks' Mastercard and Visa card bases was launched by American Express yesterday. Unlike the traditional Amex charge card - where the full balance must be paid off monthly - the new card will operate as a creditcard. It will offer customers a more competitive interest rate of 13.85 per cent - two percentage points lower than competing products. Page B3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
